body: @junov and @smaug---- might have ideas here. I think there is a vague plan to change hit regions into not requiring that feature to change the way events work, but rather just becoming ordinary event targets themselves.

On Mon, Apr 11, 2016 at 9:40 PM, Greggman notifications@github.com wrote:

> Is canvas hit region dead or is it still expected to be implemented?
> 
> Implementation is nearing completion in Blink
> 
> In any case, could this not be decoupled from canvas 2d? AFAICT the only
> connections are the currentpath and the current transform. If those 2
> things were passed in instead of inferred then hitregions would be usable
> for WebGL as well (and possibly other things).
> 
> That is a valid point. I think this feature was spec'ed before there was a
> Path2D interface, and the path option was bootstrapped later.
> 
> I suppose in the worst case you can layer a canvas 2d over a webgl canvas.
> That still brings up the speed issue though from #1029
> https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/1029 in which case you might want
> to be able to pass in a 4x4 matrix instead of the canvas 2d's 2x3 matrix

We could do something like:

HitRegionOptions {
  (...)
  DOMMatrix? transform = null;
}

When transform is null, we'd use the context's current transform (if
context is '2d', identity otherwise), this is just like how we use the
current path when 'path' is null.
DOMMatrix is a 4x4 matrix.

> —
> You are receiving this because you are subscribed to this thread.
> Reply to this email directly or view it on GitHub
> https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/1030

Hit regions are still hidden behind a flag in both Chrome and Firefox, and
AFAIK there are no other implementations.  There is likely still an
opportunity to move the HitRegion methods to HTMLCanvasElement with out
breaking the web, otherwise, we could just add "WebGLRenderingContext
implements CanvasHitRegion;" to the WebGL spec, and change some of the
wording in the hitregion spec to loosen the coupling with 2d contexts.

> I think there is a vague plan to change hit regions into not requiring that feature to change the way events work, but rather just becoming ordinary event targets themselves.

Something like that. At least I consider the event handling of hit regions totally unstable currently. Someone should try to find some time and redesign that part of the API to utilize existing features we have in the platform and not add weird pseudo-event-retargeting 

And also other parts of the API are open to even radical improvements, IMHO.

I don't have anything in my mind, but since the API hasn't shipped yet, all I'm saying it is still ok to change it if we figure out that it isn't quite what we want (like, if it doesn't work too well with webgl).
If we want to change the API, better to do it before shipping implementations.

And I think event handling is wrong, as I said in that other bug.
But if other parts of the API are ok, good.

Yes, absolutely - thanks!  Note though that shipping in blink [is imminent](https://groups.google.com/a/chromium.org/forum/#!topic/input-dev/wR-UQJxY0E8), but we're of course happy to block on any concrete efforts to improve the API.

> And I think event handling is wrong, as I said in that other bug.

Sorry, which other bug?  Perhaps I haven't seen it yet?
I think you filed it. The one about Touch and other event handling.

> Alternately, @junov your suggested change sounds reasonable to me, do you want to follow-up with Frank offline and see what he thinks and circle back here?

Sure. I'd like to keep the discussion on an open forum, so I'll use public-canvas-api@w3.org, which is where some previous amendments to hit regions were discussed in the past.

Okay, so afaict the problem with the current API is that hit regions are not objects of their own. If they were objects of their own, they could be event targets and their "get the parent" algorithm for constructing the event path would simply return the canvas element to which they are attached. We would then also not have to monkey patch various event classes.

We could then also maybe make them context-independent by decoupling some of the path stuff.

At least for Mouse event case I don't see any reason for the current monkey patching, except the hit testing part. And no need to create any magical region event targets.
Events are dispatched to getElementById(event.region); (if there is region and canvas otherwise), and
then event.target == getElementById(event.region); which makes event.region useless, unless I'm missing something here.
And Touch should behave similarly. No need to have touch.target == getElementById(tough.region)
@smaug---- I think what you're missing is that the specified `event.region` is not an ID for an object in the tree. It's just a string that that you previously registered on the `canvas` element.

it is not necessarily an object in the tree, but it can be.
"Let control be the control represented by region for this canvas element, if any."
And I think we should support only that case.

I'm curious what it really means for `control` elements. 

> **control (default null)**
> ... An element (that is a descendant of the canvas) to which events are to be routed, and which accessibility tools are to use as a surrogate for describing and interacting with this region.

Which elements are valid? `<input type="range">`?  `<video>`? `<iframe>`? some user custom shadow-dom element?
https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/scripting.html#supported-interactive-canvas-fallback-element
@smaug---- I see, but then we should change the API so that hit region takes a descendant element of `<canvas>` rather than an identifier that might correspond to an element.
oh, yeah, that could simplify the API even more.

The spec already requires the control to be a descendant of the canvas:
https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/scripting.html#the-control-represented-by-a-region

Okay, so why do we have this ID-based API rather than an Element-based API? Are we revisiting a lot of topics here?

If we just want to do minimal changes here we could remove `region` from the event classes and be done with it I suppose, but it seems potentially better to not require IDs at all.

If you want the authors of the original feature proposal (https://www.w3.org/wiki/Canvas_hit_testing) to answer that question about why it is ID-based, you'll have to ask some place else.  I tried reaching out on public-canvas-api@w3.org but no one from Microsoft has replied to that thread so far.

Sounds like someplace else isn't working out either then, but it does seem that based on that thread we should maybe look into moving hit region support to the `<canvas>` element so it works for all contexts?

Moving the APIs to <canvas> would be reasonable IMHO, but there are interop issues with the W3C snapshot (a.k.a. Canvas level 1). So I am hesitant to move on this until we get feedback from Microsoft. The risk is that if we make changes without their knowledge, they could concurrently ship an incompatible implementation based on the old spec.
I have informed Adrian and Frank: https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/www-archive/2016Apr/0000.html.

Per their reply it seems they would be okay with changing the API. Note also that having non-node objects complicates `event.composedPath()` per https://github.com/w3c/webcomponents/issues/432. It would be nice to avoid that.
I just assigned this issue to myself, but it will probably be a few months before get to it.  If anyone else wants to take this over and get the spec change done sooner, please go ahead.

`Okay, so why do we have this ID-based API rather than an Element-based API? Are we revisiting a lot of topics here?`

The ID-based API is there in case the user doesn't want to create the hidden fallback elements. The idea was to make it as easy as possible to make canvas accessible.
With the ID-based API you can quickly create accessible regions while the element-based API requires you to create them, add them to the canvas, keep track of them, etc

Right. Because we have the "unbacked region description" approach for assigning ARIA roles, along with the "virtual DOM tree" representation for unbacked hit regions.  This seems like a convenience feature that adds a lot of complexity to the spec and to eventual implementations.

yes. The argument was that it gives authors an easy way to add accessibility.
When I added this to firefox, it didn't seem to make the implementation that more complex...

It IS weird that there's 2 ways of adding a11y

The .region stuff is just odd pseudo-event-retargeting and I strongly think we should get rid of it.
The implementation in Gecko is a bit buggy, and .region isn't implemented at all for Touch.
And I don't quite see reason for the added complexity when using plain normal DOM elements works fine. And supporting .region in case of shadow DOM becomes rather tricky. Makes no sense to leak .region from shadow DOM to light DOM. If we used DOM elements always, the normal dom event dispatch deals with shadow DOM stuff just fine.

And the spec isn't clear what should happen with WheelEvents or PointerEvents (Gecko implementation doesn't deal with those). Those are MouseEvents via inheritance.
I think we need to have some generic hook for hit testing and then retargeting at that level to some hit region element and then do normal DOM event dispatch there, no matter which event type is being dispatched.
I don't feel strongly about having this feature so I defer to the platform experts such as yourself to make this call.

Other option is to only use .region and never do things like "If there is a control, then target the event object at control instead of the canvas element.", so never use any element here, just target event to canvas element the normal way, and only update .region string property when needed.
And .region would be null if event.target isn't in the same node tree as event.currentTarget -
that would deal with shadow DOM.

It is mostly the current setup in the spec where there are two distinct models for hit regions which is weird. One should be enough.

Are there any links to some discussions leading to the current design?

I found a discussion where we discussed why the ID base approach is needed: https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/public-canvas-api/2014JanMar/0188.html

A11y minutes are also posted in the mailing list. (Sorry, I don't remember all the details)

Thanks.

Ok, the id based API was a concern already back then. and there is a comment "I'd actually recommend just scrapping the ID concept altogether and focus on the control nodes."
And the counter argument to that, well, it doesn't explain at all why controls wouldn't work just fine.

So, many people were mostly favoring controls-only approach back then, and still are. And there hasn't been strong arguments why we need this model with ID and controls.
Besides, using controls only makes the model closer to the old style img's usemap.
I assume in Gecko we'd use similar implementation for the control stuff as what we use for usemap, at least for hit testing. (I don't see any of that been implemented in Gecko currently.)

From my comment in 2014:
'For instance, if you draw a dialog with a button on top of other controls,
you will need to create a region the size of the dialog to obscure the
controls at a  lower z-order'

So, if you want to obscure accessible region but don't want to provide a control (because it's just color), you need to create something like the id-based approach. An author could of course remove the controls but that's a bit cumbersome

HitRegion has been removed from this spec -> closing this issue.
Onlookers: be on the lookout for an alternative proposal at W3C (WICG perhaps?)
@junov my commit specifically left this open for the follow-up work. I think it'll have to be integrated in HTML at some point so we might as well keep this as a tracking issue.
@junov is there anything to point at yet?
Not to my knowledge. This is burried is pretty deep in my TODO list.  If other contributors would like to take the initiative, please do.

I created a revised proposal for hit regions that takes into account WebGL: #3407. It doesn't yet take into account #1029, but it would be fairly easy to do so in a future revision, once there's some implementation interest. I'm going to close this issue therefore and encourage everyone to review #3407.
